stance.label: Watch
stance.oneLine: The most leveraged of the three: five times EBITDA gross, interest covered barely once in the first half, AED 5.5 bn lent to affiliates outside the rated group — offset by Sharjah government support, a AED 15.5 bn backlog and bonds that still trade near par.

Sharjah's largest master-plan developer; one-notch uplift for government support; governance negative

strengths: Sharjah's dominant master-plan developer (about half of the emirate's off-plan volume) in a more affordable, end-user market — Moody's: 'unique market position in Sharjah'
Government of Sharjah is a 40% shareholder and land creditor on deferred terms; Fitch rates the sukuk a notch above the standalone for that support
IFRS backlog AED 15.5 bn, of which AED 6.8 bn falls due within a year; gross margins near 40%
AED 3.7 bn of cash and deposits, AED 2.3 bn of it outside escrow, against USD 412m of sukuk due in June 2027
Market access intact: the 2030 sukuk was four times covered at 7.15% and all three issues still trade near par
concerns: Leverage is out of line with the ratings: five times LTM EBITDA gross; Moody's says it is 'elevated for the rating level' and Fitch's downgrade line is 4.5x
Interest cover thinned to 1.2x gross in H1 2026 (finance cost AED 419m against adjusted EBITDA AED 503m); covenant compliance leans on AED 205m of interest income charged to affiliates

AED 5.5 bn is owed to the rated company by affiliates — chiefly a AED 3.5 bn 7% loan to Arada Group LLC due December 2027 — more than its entire equity, and the shareholders ceased to jointly control that group in February 2026; the international expansion (London AED 2.5 bn, Australia, a USD 7 bn Syria venture, a hospital) sits there
Cash from operations was AED 7m in the half; Sharjah plans collect 60–70% at handover, so liquidity is a handover schedule — and management blames the conflict for material delays
Covenants were loosened in 2025 when the first vote fell short; a second consent in 2026 seeks a call right to refinance the 2027 paper
Moody's: 'relatively limited operating track record … alongside past delays'; a board with one independent director

view.capacity: Arada can pay the June 2027 sukuk from cash on hand today — AED 2.3 billion outside escrow against AED 1.5 billion due — and the company is already lining up a refinancing by adding a call right. What it cannot do comfortably is carry its debt on current earnings: the first half produced AED 503 million of EBITDA against AED 419 million of finance cost and AED 7 million of operating cash flow. The credit works only if the AED 6.8 billion of backlog due within a year hands over on schedule, because Sharjah buyers pay most of the price at the door.
view.refinancing: The bonds price none of this stress: 6–7.5% yields are the tightest of the three issuers, reflecting the Sharjah government's 40% stake and land support more than the accounts. That support is the reason a refinancing of the 2027 paper should get done, most likely by a new sukuk once the call right passes on 17 September, or by bank facilities secured on Aljada receivables if the market stays shut. The cost will be higher than 8.125% if either agency moves first: Moody's outlook is negative and Fitch is on watch.
view.restructuring: A restructuring is not the base case while the shareholders keep funding and the government keeps deferring, but this is the issuer where the question is fair to ask. The mechanism would be leakage: cash raised by the rated company flowing to affiliates outside the rating perimeter (AED 803 million net in the first half) while its own interest cover sits near one. Watch the affiliate receivable, the September consent result, whether H2 2026 handovers recover from the delays management has admitted, and any Moody's move to B2.
view.forBuyers: Escrow protects deposits in Sharjah as in Dubai, and Arada has delivered more than 10,000 homes since 2017. The realistic risk to an off-plan buyer is a later key date: the company has acknowledged supply-chain delays in 2026 and has an incentive to prioritise projects nearest handover. Buyers should check the delay history of their specific phase rather than the group's headline.
